bugClass.title: Unsettled in-flight queue attempt blocks later work
bugClass.cause: A single-slot queue consumer allows an adapter exception to escape without settling or clearing the current attempt. The slot remains occupied, so later ticks replay the same failed attempt and never reach queued work.
bugClass.criteria: Classify another site when it has a single in-flight slot or equivalent serialized consumer and either (a) an adapter/send operation can throw before the attempt is settled or the slot cleared, causing repeated replay and blocking later work, or (b) a tick retries an already occupied slot without advancing or releasing it. Either path independently qualifies.

candidates.evidence: `replayState` reads the current `state.inFlight` and clears it when the issued attempt is stale or parked (lines 153–157). Otherwise it returns the same `issued` attempt, but the excerpt does not show a tick retrying it or whether any later work is blocked.

A serialized promise queue exists (`this.queue`), and `send()` chains `session.exchange(text, this.timeoutMs)` (lines 28–46). The excerpt ends before showing how the queue is updated or how exchange failures are handled, so it does not establish a stuck slot or replay that blocks later work.

The excerpt shows a current sink slot that `release()` clears, and `end()` releases the current sink (lines 58–73). Although `deliver()` calls `sink.send(...)`, the excerpt does not show the queued-attempt or receive settlement path, so it cannot establish an exception leaving a serialized attempt occupied.

At line 163, completion deletes state.inFlight after dispatching the result to a type-specific completion function. The excerpt does not show how a failed adapter/send or a retry tick behaves before this completion path, so it cannot establish a stuck slot or replay trigger.

`RelayLinkService.command` calls `send` before creating and registering the acknowledgement timer/entry (lines 50–58), so a synchronous socket-send exception could reject the promise before a slot is recorded. The excerpt shows no single in-flight queue slot or replay tick, and does not establish that later queued work is blocked.

`WireClientService` sends waiting requests in a loop after attachment (lines 52–59); `unbind` rejects and clears the attaching request and `close` settles all waiting requests in the excerpt. It does not show a single serialized in-flight slot or retrying tick, nor whether a thrown `send` strands later work.
At line 131, inFlight is an optional DeliveryAttempt field in the state type. This establishes a possible slot but shows no consumer, send operation, retry tick, or missing settlement guard.

At lines 42–51, `exchange` creates a promise, starts or reuses a child, and assigns `waiting` before writing to stdin. The excerpt does not show whether a synchronous `stdin.write` exception settles the promise or clears `waiting`, nor whether this is a queue consumer that blocks later work.

At lines 74–89, `runJob` avoids starting work when `jobs.busy()` reports occupied, observes claimed work, and settles after obtaining a receipt. The excerpt does not show what happens if `jobReceipt` throws before settlement or whether later ticks retry the same claimed item and block queued work.

`HostLinkService.welcome` sends the ready frame, then each open connection/request, then notifies host-online (lines 52–55). The excerpt does not show a single in-flight queue slot, retry tick, or any guard/settlement behavior if a socket send throws.

At lines 17–26, the socket's `send` is called when its state is open, while the connection promise has a rejection handler. The excerpt does not show any queue slot or settlement behavior if `socket.send(text)` throws, or a tick that replays an occupied attempt.

At lines 63–80, `framing.send` delegates to `socket.send`, and `receive` catches framing/receive errors by closing the socket. This excerpt does not establish a single-slot queue attempt or show how a send exception affects queued work.

Lines 52–64 show `hello()` calls `options.send` when a device is unknown, then drops the address. The excerpt does not establish a single in-flight slot or recurring tick, nor whether a throwing send is caught or blocks later work.

Lines 51–54 validate a persisted `harness_notification_inflight` table with a single `slot` column, suggesting a single-slot attempt. The excerpt does not show the consumer, adapter/send failure path, or whether occupied attempts are retried without settlement, so the blocking cause is not established.
